# Task: Complete Phase 7 only (Cloud architecture, IaC, CI/CD definitions)

Work autonomously and finish in one pass. Do not ask me questions or stop for approval. If something is ambiguous, choose the simplest option that meets the plan and note it in one line in the docs.

## Scope
Do only what Phase 7 in `docs/implementation-plan.md` lists in work packages 1 to 6, plus the draw.io diagram and documentation sync below. Add nothing else. Do not touch application code or Phase 8 or 9 content.

Read only these first:
- `docs/implementation-plan.md` (Phase 7)
- `docs/architecture/decisions/adr-0007-demo-delivery-mode.md`
- `.github/instructions/bicep-code-best-practices.instructions.md`
- `.github/instructions/ci-security.instructions.md`
- `.github/agents/azure-verified-modules-bicep.agent.md`
- `.github/workflows/validate.yml` (reuse its check commands)
- `docs/architecture/architecture-overview.md` ("Deployment view" and "Local-to-cloud component mapping")
- The existing `Containerfile`, `apps/web/Containerfile`, and `compose.yaml`

## Boundary: author and validate only, never deploy
- Do not run `az deployment ... create`, `az group create`, `az login`, or anything that creates, changes, or deletes Azure resources.
- Run `az deployment sub what-if` only if `az account show` already works without a login prompt. Otherwise skip it and record "what-if skipped: no authenticated subscription".
- No secrets, `.env` values, or real subscription, tenant, or client IDs. Use placeholders. Never put secrets in Bicep parameters.

## Deliverables
1. `infra/bicep/main.bicep` (subscription scope, creates the resource group) with modules for:
   - network: VNet, subnets for Container Apps and private endpoints, NSGs, NAT Gateway
   - platform: Log Analytics, Application Insights, Key Vault, ACR
   - Container Apps environment with `api` and `web` apps and a weekly cron ingestion job
   - Cosmos DB for MongoDB, Storage queue, Azure AI Search, each with a private endpoint and private DNS zone
   - user-assigned managed identity with least-privilege role assignments
   - Foundry endpoint and deployment names as parameters only
   - APIM as an optional module behind `deployApim` (default `false`)

   Use pinned AVM modules where one fits. Otherwise write a small plain module rather than fighting AVM. Also add `infra/bicep/parameters/dev.bicepparam` and `infra/bicep/bicepconfig.json`.
2. `infra/README.md` with the naming pattern `{type}-psa-{env}-cac-{nn}`, the mandatory tags table, and the one-time bootstrap (Entra app registration and federated credentials for the `dev` environment, with required repo variables and secrets by name only). Start it with this scope note:
   > Scope note: this IaC is validated by build, lint and static review only and has not been deployed. It shows the intended Azure architecture. Production gates (policy scanning, structural checks, cost estimate, APIM SKU choice, branch protection) are recorded in the Phase 7 "Production-only" note and in `docs/operations/production-gap-register.md`. The focus was a working local application first.
3. `.github/workflows/infra.yml`: on pull request to `infra/**`, run `bicep build`, `bicep lint`, and `what-if` (skipped when the OIDC secrets are absent). A deploy job runs on `workflow_dispatch` only, uses the `dev` environment, and authenticates with `azure/login` using OIDC.
4. `.github/workflows/app.yml`: run the Python and web checks, build the container images, and push to ACR on `main`. Deploy to Container Apps on `workflow_dispatch` with the `dev` environment.
5. In all workflows, pin every action by full 40-character SHA with a version comment. Resolve SHAs with `gh api` or `git ls-remote`, never guess. Use `permissions: contents: read` by default and `id-token: write` only on jobs that need it.
6. **Azure infrastructure diagram (draw.io).** Create the diagram after the Bicep is final, so that it matches the Bicep exactly. Use only resources that the Bicep defines.
   - Files: `docs/architecture/diagrams/azure-infrastructure.drawio.svg` (editable draw.io SVG with the diagram embedded). Keep the source `.drawio` alongside it only if the export needs it.
   - Show these segregation zones as labelled containers:
     - **Internet / external**: users, public documentation hosts, Foundry endpoint (the demo uses its public endpoint), and GitHub Actions (OIDC to Azure).
     - **Resource group > VNet** with its address space, containing:
       - the **Container Apps subnet** (NSG shown): Container Apps environment with `web`, `api`, and the weekly ingestion job
       - the **private endpoint subnet** (NSG shown): private endpoints for Cosmos DB for MongoDB, Storage queue, Azure AI Search, Key Vault, and ACR (include only those the Bicep creates)
       - **NAT Gateway** with its public IP as the only outbound path from the Container Apps subnet
     - **Private DNS zones**, linked to the VNet, one per private endpoint type.
     - **Platform and identity services**: Log Analytics, Application Insights, user-assigned managed identity (with its main role assignments), and an optional APIM box drawn dashed and labelled "deployApim = false".
   - Show the direction of traffic with arrows: user to `web`, `web` to `api`, `api` to private endpoints, ingestion job to the NAT Gateway and then to the public documentation hosts, and `api` to Foundry through the NAT Gateway. Add a short legend (solid for runtime traffic, dashed for optional or not deployed).
   - Label the title "Designed in Bicep, not deployed".
   - Export with the draw.io desktop CLI, for example `& "C:\Program Files\draw.io\draw.io.exe" -x -f svg --embed-diagram -o docs/architecture/diagrams/azure-infrastructure.drawio.svg <source.drawio>`. If the CLI fails, retry with `--no-sandbox`. If it still fails, keep the `.drawio` source, record "image export skipped" in the Phase 7 status, and keep a Mermaid version of the cloud design in the architecture overview as the fallback.
   - Embed it in `docs/architecture/architecture-overview.md` under "Deployment view" with `![Azure infrastructure, designed in Bicep, not deployed](diagrams/azure-infrastructure.drawio.svg)` and one sentence on how the network is segregated. Replace the old conceptual "Cloud" subgraph in the Mermaid diagram so that the two diagrams do not contradict each other. Keep the local developer part of that Mermaid diagram. Update the "Local-to-cloud component mapping" rows that now have a Bicep counterpart.

## Validation (run it yourself, fix failures, re-run until clean)
1. `az bicep build --file infra/bicep/main.bicep` and `az bicep build-params --file infra/bicep/parameters/dev.bicepparam`
2. `az bicep lint --file infra/bicep/main.bicep` (zero errors; one-line justification for any remaining warning)
3. `podman run --rm -v "${PWD}:/repo" -w /repo docker.io/rhysd/actionlint:latest -color`. If the image cannot be pulled, do a YAML parse check and record that actionlint was skipped.
4. Confirm that every `uses:` in the new workflows is SHA-pinned.
5. Diagram check: the exported SVG exists and is well-formed XML, the markdown image path resolves, and every resource on the diagram appears in the Bicep (and the reverse, for the resources listed in deliverable 6).

## Documentation sync (only what Phase 7 changes)
Search the docs for "Phase 7", "Bicep", "infra/", "IaC", and "CI/CD". Update a doc only when a statement there is now stale or contradicts what you built. Keep each edit to one or two lines, and do not rewrite sections.
- `README.md`: add links to `infra/README.md`, the two new workflows, and the infrastructure diagram.
- `docs/architecture/decision-register.md` and `requirements-traceability.md`: mark the IaC and CI/CD items as authored and statically validated, not deployed.
- `docs/security/security-posture.md`: mark the cloud network, identity and private endpoint rows as "designed in Bicep, not deployed".
- `docs/security/threat-register.md`: add at most two threats introduced by this phase (OIDC federation scope, ACR push permissions), each with a one-line control or a "production-only" note.
- `docs/operations/production-gap-register.md`: add a line only if a Phase 7 "Production-only" item is missing. Do not duplicate existing lines.
- `docs/implementation-plan.md`: update the Phase 7 **Status** line with the date, the commands run, and the results. Say plainly which checks passed and which were skipped, and why. Do not claim a check passed unless you ran it.

## Finish
- Do not commit or push. Leave changes in the working tree.
- Reply in at most 8 lines: files added, files updated, validation results, and any decision I should know about.

 ---
 title: ADR-0007 Demo Delivery Mode
 description: Lighter governance for the working local demo, with production-only controls recorded rather than performed
 author: Product Support Agent Team
 ms.date: 2026-11-22
 ms.topic: decision
 keywords:
   - ADR
   - governance
   - delivery
   - production readiness
 ---
 
 ## Status
 
 Accepted by the user on 2026-11-22. This ADR supersedes the per-phase approval
 loop described in earlier versions of the
 [implementation plan](../../implementation-plan.md).
 
 ## Context
 
 The goal is a working local demo that runs end to end against real Azure
 resources (Microsoft Foundry models and Azure AI Search). The demo is followed
 by CI/CD definitions for IaC and for build and deployment. The demo exists to
 show web and agentic architecture skills. It is not meant to be a
 production-ready application.
 
 The earlier plan required explicit approval before every phase, every live
 request batch, and every exit item. That loop cost more time than the risk it
 controlled. Phases stalled on approvals that matter only before a production
 release.
 
 ## Decision
 
 ### Delivery mode
 
 The project runs in **demo delivery mode** until a production decision is
 made. In this mode, a contributor, human or coding agent, may proceed through
 Phases 4 to 7 without asking for approval, as long as the guardrails below hold.
 
 ### Guardrails that always apply
 
 These are cheap, protect real systems, and stay in force in demo mode:
 
 1. Never commit secrets, `.env`, scraped content, or MongoDB data.
 2. Anonymous access only. Never authenticate to, or bypass, a protected source.
 3. Fetch source content only from the versioned
    [source map](../../operations/phase-3-source-map-v1.json), through the
    source worker, which enforces `robots.txt`, request budgets, and backoff.
 4. Keep citations bound to retrieved evidence. The model never authors URLs.
 5. Keep query/response retention off (`QUERY_RESPONSE_RETENTION_ENABLED=false`).
 6. Bind local services to loopback. Do not expose the demo publicly.
 7. Keep routine tests offline (fakes and mocks). Live tests are opt-in with
    `-m live`.
 8. Keep `ruff`, `mypy`, `pytest`, `bandit`, and the web checks passing.
 
 ### Pre-authorized actions
 
 Actions authorized for the demo without further approval:
 
 | Action | Limit |
 |---|---|
 | Live documentation ingestion with `scripts/run_source_ingestion.py` | The default budget (400 requests per run), at most one run per day; a weekly schedule is fine |
 | Calls to the user-provided Foundry chat and embedding deployments in `.env` | Demo and test traffic only; keep batches small |
 | Creating, updating, or deleting indexes in the user-provided Azure AI Search service | Index names must start with `product-support-` |
 | Live integration tests against a `product-support-test-*` index | Opt-in with `pytest -m live` |
 | Local Podman containers for this project | The project's `compose.yaml` services only; do not touch other projects' containers |
 | Authoring Bicep, GitHub Actions workflows, and pipeline definitions | Authoring and static validation (`az bicep build`, `what-if` where possible) |
 
 ### Actions that still need the user
 
 * Creating or changing Azure resources other than the Search indexes above,
   including deploying the network slice or the application.
 * Spending outside the existing deployments, such as new model deployments or
   SKU changes.
 * Adding a new source host or product to the source map.
 * Enabling query/response retention.
 
 ### Deferred to production
 
 The following controls are part of a production-grade delivery. They are
 **recorded and designed, not performed** for the demo, and do not block any
 demo phase:
 
 | Area | Production expectation | Demo treatment |
 |---|---|---|
 | Phase gates | Formal exit review and sign-off per phase | Exit criteria are the definition of done; no sign-off loop |
 | Source terms | Legal review of documentation reuse terms | Public, `robots.txt`-permitted docs used for a private, non-commercial demo; review before any public or commercial use |
 | Retrieval quality | Reviewed, versioned relevance set with agreed thresholds and sign-off | Small synthetic evaluation set with the documented thresholds (Phase 6); no human review panel |
 | Semantic reranking | Measured decision against the reviewed set | Off by default; may be enabled if the Search tier allows it, noted in the plan |
 | Usability | Moderated study with representative users | Self-walkthrough of the five demo tasks |
 | Accessibility | Automated scans plus manual keyboard and screen-reader review against WCAG 2.2 AA | Semantic HTML, labels, and keyboard checks; a full audit is deferred |
 | Privacy | Approved notice, reviewer access, redaction, TTL, and deletion before retention | Retention stays off |
 | Threat model | Every high-rated threat tested or formally accepted per phase | Register maintained; tests for the guardrails above; remaining threats noted as production work |
 | Identity | Entra ID, managed identity, and keyless access to Search and Foundry | API keys from `.env` |
 | Network | Private endpoints, VNet, and controlled egress | Public endpoints from the developer machine |
 | Observability | OpenTelemetry to Azure Monitor with retention policy | Structured, redacted logs; optional local tracing |
 | Supply chain | Branch protection, required checks, image scanning, provenance | CI workflow runs checks; branch protection is a backlog item |
 | Operations | SLOs, on-call, incident response, backup and restore | Not applicable to a local demo |
 
 ## Consequences
 
 * Phases 4 to 7 can be completed in sequence without waiting for approvals,
   within the guardrails and pre-authorized actions.
 * The documentation still shows the production path: each deferred control has
   a design or an entry in the threat register, the security posture, or the
   production gap register (Phase 9).
 * Any move toward production, a public demo, or customer data reopens the
   deferred controls. They then become blocking.
 
 ## Alternatives considered
 
 * Keep per-phase approval: rejected, because it was the main delay and
   protected nothing that mattered for a private demo.
 * Drop the governance documentation entirely: rejected, because the
   documentation shows that the production controls are understood.

diff --git a/C:/ubk-repos/product-support-agent/.github/instructions/bicep-code-best-practices.instructions.md b/C:/ubk-repos/product-support-agent/.github/instructions/bicep-code-best-practices.instructions.md
index 0000000..0000000 100644
--- a/C:/ubk-repos/product-support-agent/.github/instructions/bicep-code-best-practices.instructions.md
+++ b/C:/ubk-repos/product-support-agent/.github/instructions/bicep-code-best-practices.instructions.md
@@ -1,74 +1,74 @@
 ---
 description: 'Infrastructure as Code with Bicep'
 applyTo: '**/*.bicep, **/*.bicepparam, **/bicepconfig.json'
 ---
 
 ## Project constraints
 
 - Follow the Phase 7 scope and approval gates in `docs/implementation-plan.md`.
 - The application stack is design-only. Do not deploy it or run subscription-scoped validation without explicit approval.
 - Pin suitable AVM versions, design for Canada Central, and keep the separately approved network slice distinct from the full stack.
 
 ## Naming Conventions
 
 -   When writing Bicep code, use lowerCamelCase for all names (variables, parameters, resources)
 -   Use resource type descriptive symbolic names (e.g., 'storageAccount' not 'storageAccountName')
 -   Avoid using 'name' in a symbolic name as it represents the resource, not the resource's name
 -   Avoid distinguishing variables and parameters by the use of suffixes
 
 ## Structure and Declaration
 
 -   Always declare parameters at the top of files with @description decorators
 -   Prefer supported stable API versions verified against current documentation; preserve existing versions during unrelated changes
 -   Use descriptive @description decorators for all parameters
 -   Specify minimum and maximum character length for naming parameters
 
 ## Parameters
 
 -   Set default values that are safe for test environments (use low-cost pricing tiers)
 -   Use @allowed decorator sparingly to avoid blocking valid deployments
 -   Use parameters for settings that change between deployments
 -   Use `.bicepparam` files with a `using` declaration when supported by the project's tool versions; retain JSON parameter files where required. Keep secrets out of parameter files and use supported secret references.
 -   Use supported user-defined object types for structured parameter contracts when they make validation clearer.
 
 ## Modules and Validation
 
 -   Prefer an appropriate Azure Verified Module when it meets the project's requirements, and reference a specific module version. Preserve existing module versions during unrelated changes.
 -   Respect the project's Bicep CLI version and `bicepconfig.json` linter settings. Run the project's Bicep build/lint checks before deployment, and resolve diagnostics rather than disabling rules globally.
 
 ## Variables
 
 -   Variables automatically infer type from the resolved value
 -   Use variables to contain complex expressions instead of embedding them directly in resource properties
 
 ## Resource References
 
 -   Use symbolic names for resource references instead of reference() or resourceId() functions
 -   Create resource dependencies through symbolic names (resourceA.id) not explicit dependsOn
 -   For accessing properties from other resources, use the 'existing' keyword instead of passing values through outputs
 
 ## Resource Names
 
 -   Use template expressions with uniqueString() to create meaningful and unique resource names
 -   Add prefixes to uniqueString() results since some resources don't allow names starting with numbers
 
 ## Child Resources
 
 -   Avoid excessive nesting of child resources
 -   Use parent property or nesting instead of constructing resource names for child resources
 
 ## Security
 
 -   Never include secrets or keys in outputs
 -   Use resource properties directly in outputs (e.g., storageAccount.properties.primaryEndpoints)
 
 ## Documentation
 
 -   Explain non-obvious decisions with concise comments where needed
 
 ## References
 
 -   [Bicep modules and Azure Verified Modules](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-resource-manager/bicep/modules)
 -   [Bicep parameter files](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-resource-manager/bicep/parameter-files)
 -   [Bicep linter](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-resource-manager/bicep/linter)

index 0000000..0000000 100644
--- a/C:/ubk-repos/product-support-agent/.github/instructions/ci-security.instructions.md
+++ b/C:/ubk-repos/product-support-agent/.github/instructions/ci-security.instructions.md
@@ -1,16 +1,16 @@
 ---
 description: "Security requirements for future GitHub Actions workflows"
 applyTo: ".github/workflows/**/*.{yml,yaml},.github/workflows/*.{yml,yaml}"
 ---
 
 # GitHub Actions security
 
 Follow the approval gates and workflow separation in `docs/implementation-plan.md`. Do not enable application deployment as part of the MVP.
 
 * Pin every external action to a verified full commit SHA, including first-party actions.
 * Set explicit least-privilege permissions. Grant `id-token: write` only to jobs that need approved OIDC authentication.
 * Treat pull request metadata, artifacts, and caches as untrusted. Do not interpolate untrusted values directly into shell scripts or run untrusted code in privileged workflows.
 * Do not expose secrets to untrusted code. Disable checkout credential persistence when it is not required.
 * Restrict deployment to an approved manual workflow and protected environment. The full application deployment remains disabled.
 * Validate workflows with the approved tooling and review triggers, runner trust, dependencies, permissions, and cloud identity boundaries.

 # Azure AVM Bicep mode
 
 Use Azure Verified Modules for Bicep to enforce Azure best practices via pre-built modules.
 
 Follow `docs/implementation-plan.md`: Phase 7 is design-only for the application stack. Do not deploy or run subscription-scoped validation without explicit approval. The separately approved network slice is the only planned deployment; confirm its cost and teardown plan first.
 
 ## Discover modules
 
 - AVM Index: `https://azure.github.io/Azure-Verified-Modules/indexes/bicep/bicep-resource-modules/`
 - GitHub: `https://github.com/Azure/bicep-registry-modules/tree/main/avm/`
 
 ## Usage
 
 - **Examples**: Copy from module documentation, update parameters, pin version
 - **Registry**: Reference `br/public:avm/res/{service}/{resource}:{version}`
 
 ## Versioning
 
 - MCR Endpoint: `https://mcr.microsoft.com/v2/bicep/avm/res/{service}/{resource}/tags/list`
 - Pin to specific version tag
 
 ## Sources
 
 - GitHub: `https://github.com/Azure/bicep-registry-modules/tree/main/avm/res/{service}/{resource}`
 - Registry: `br/public:avm/res/{service}/{resource}:{version}`
 
 ## Naming conventions
 
 - Resource: avm/res/{service}/{resource}
 - Pattern: avm/ptn/{pattern}
 - Utility: avm/utl/{utility}
 
 ## Best practices
 
 - Prefer AVM modules where available and suitable; use thin composition or native resources when needed
 - Pin module versions
 - Start with official examples
 - Review module parameters and outputs
 - Always run `bicep lint` after making changes
 - Verify service availability, schema, SKU, identity, network and DNS requirements against current official Microsoft documentation

Every request is counted against the run's budget and spaced at least 1 second apart per host. ```mermaid flowchart TD Start([Scheduled or manual run]) --> Lease{Acquire MongoDB lease} Lease -->|Held by another run| Exit3([Exit code 3]) Lease -->|Acquired| Next{Next enabled source?} Next -->|None| Report([Write metadata-only report, release lease]) Next -->|Source| ProductBackoff{Product in fail-fast backoff?} ProductBackoff -->|Yes| Next ProductBackoff -->|No| HostAborted{Host aborted this run?} HostAborted -->|Yes| Next HostAborted -->|No| SeedFresh{Seed fetched within 24 h

or revision unchanged?} Fresh -->|Yes| Skip[Skip without a request] Skip --> Page Fresh -->|No| Allowed{robots.txt allows fetch
and citation URL?} Allowed -->|No| Disallowed["Record robots_disallowed, 30-day backoff"] Disallowed --> Page Allowed -->|Yes| Get[Conditional GET, at most 2 attempts] Get -->|304 or same body hash| Unchanged[Record unchanged] Unchanged --> Page Get -->|429| AbortHost Get -->|Protected, 4xx, oversized| Permanent["30-day backoff"] Get -->|5xx, network, indexing error| Transient["Backoff 1, 2, 4, then 7 days"] Permanent --> Streak{3 consecutive failures?} Transient --> Streak Streak -->|Yes| FailFast[Fail product fast, back it off] FailFast --> Next Streak -->|No| Page Get -->|200, new content| Extract[Extract HTML from JSON or main content] Extract --> Normalize[Normalize, chunk, persist with fetched_at] Normalize --> Record[Record indexed state] Record --> Page ``` Each request's state is written to `source_fetch_state` as soon as the request finishes. A restarted run therefore skips URLs that succeeded within the freshness window. If that write was lost, the canonical document's `fetched_at` is a second guard. ## Restart and resume sequence ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber participant Sched as Scheduler participant Run as Source worker participant State as MongoDB source_fetch_state participant Docs as MongoDB canonical_documents participant Site as Documentation host Sched->>Run: Run 1 Run->>Site: robots.txt, TOC, page 1, page 2 Run->>State: Indexed: page 1, then page 2 Run->>Docs: Upsert page 1 and page 2 documents Note over Run: Crash before page 3 Sched->>Run: Run 2, minutes later Run->>State: Read seed: fresh, use stored page list Run->>State: Page 1 and page 2: success within 24 h Note over Run,Site: No requests for pages 1 and 2 Run->>State: Page 3: no record Run->>Docs: Page 3 fetched_at? none Run->>Site: GET page 3 Run->>Docs: Upsert page 3 Run->>State: Record page 3 indexed Sched->>Run: Weekly run Run->>Site: Conditional GET TOC, If-None-Match Site-->>Run: 200 with revisions Note over Run: Unchanged revisions skip without a request Run->>Site: Conditional GET changed pages only ``` ## never contains page content | | Canonical documents and chunks | MongoDB `canonical_documents`, `canonical_chunks` | System of record; not committed to git | | Searchable chunks and vectors | Azure AI Search, versioned index | Derived; rebuilt from MongoDB | | Queue messages | Azurite | Product references only | | Run and coverage reports | JSON output, API responses | Outcomes and counts only | ## Trust boundaries Edge labels use the boundary IDs from the [threat register](../security/threat-register.md#trust-boundaries). ```mermaid flowchart LR Browser[User browser] subgraph Local["Local application, loopback-bound"] UI[Next.js] API[FastAPI] Agent["Agent"] Worker[Source and queue workers] Mongo[(MongoDB)] Queue[(Azurite)] Retention[("Retention collection, off by default")] end subgraph Public["Untrusted public sources"] Docs[Documentation hosts] Catalog[OpenText catalog feed] end subgraph Microsoft["User-provided Microsoft services"] Search[Azure AI Search] Foundry[Foundry deployments] end Telemetry["Telemetry collector, not selected"] DevCreds["Developer credentials and config"] Browser -->|"TB-01: HTML only, no history"| UI UI -->|"TB-02: server-side fetch"| API API --> Agent Agent -->|"TB-03: prompts and evidence"| Foundry Worker -->|"TB-04: allowlist, robots, no redirects, limits"| Docs API -.->|"TB-04: one-time manifest"| Catalog Worker -->|"TB-05: state, documents, references"| Mongo Worker --> Queue API -->|"TB-05: read fetch state"| Mongo Worker -->|"TB-06: chunks and vectors"| Search Agent -->|"TB-06: hybrid queries"| Search API -.->|"TB-07: content-free events"| Telemetry API -.->|"Only after privacy approval and opt-in"| Retention DevCreds -.->|"TB-08"| Search ``` Source text, user input, and model output are untrusted. TB-09, the cloud application boundary, is design-only and is shown in the deployment view. ## Deployment view ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph Dev["Developer machine"] subgraph Podman["Podman compose, implemented"] Mongo[(MongoDB 8)] Azurite[(Azurite)] end subgraph Processes["Podman Compose services"] NextJS["Next.js on 127.0.0.1:3000"] FastAPI["FastAPI on 127.0.0.1:8000"] Job["Source ingestion job
one-shot command"] end end Search[(User-provided Azure AI Search)] Foundry[(User-provided Foundry)] Docs[(Public documentation hosts)] NextJS --> FastAPI FastAPI --> Mongo Job --> Mongo Job --> Docs Job --> Search FastAPI --> Search subgraph Cloud["Conceptual Azure design, not deployed"] APIM[APIM] ACA["Container Apps: UI, API, scheduled ingestion job"] Data[Cosmos DB for MongoDB, Storage queue, AI Search] Egress[NAT Gateway egress with allowlist] Obs[Azure Monitor] APIM --> ACA ACA --> Data ACA --> Egress ACA --> Obs end ``` The application stack is not deployed to Azure. A network slice is a distinct, later-approved activity described in Phase 7 of the [implementation plan](../implementation-plan.md). ## Local-to-cloud component mapping | Local MVP | Conceptual Azure counterpart | Important difference or limit | |---|---|---| | Next.js UI | Container App | Application deployment is deferred; cloud user authentication is not yet decided. | | FastAPI and agent | Container App | Cloud identity and APIM behavior require Phase 7 validation. | | Source ingestion job, weekly task | Container Apps job on a cron schedule | Egress must be allowlisted; the MongoDB lease keeps runs single-instance. | | Catalog process and queue worker | Container App with queue-based scaling | Used for manifest creation; not needed for weekly documentation refresh. | | Direct Foundry OpenAI-compatible calls | Azure API Management | LiteLLM is optional for the demo; gateway policy and managed identity are production work. | | MongoDB | Cosmos DB for MongoDB | Authentication, `tz_aware` datetimes, and atomic upserts for the lease must be verified. | | Azurite Queue | Azure Storage Queue | Poison-message and completion tracking need application-level handling. | | Azure AI Search | Azure AI Search | Same provider. Local access uses the public endpoint; the cloud design uses a private endpoint. | | No response cache | Azure Cache for Redis only if justified | Source fetch state is an idempotency control, not a cache. | | Collector not selected | Azure Monitor and Log Analytics | Query and response content is excluded until privacy approval. | ## References * [ADR-0002 Source access and manifest](decisions/adr-0002-source-access-and-manifest.md) * [ADR-0006 Periodic, resumable documentation ingestion](decisions/adr-0006-periodic-resumable-source-ingestion.md) * [Microsoft Agent Framework overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/agent-framework/overview/) * [Azure AI Search hybrid search](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/search/hybrid-search-overview) * [RFC 9309 Robots Exclusion Protocol](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309)

 ### Phase 7: Cloud architecture, IaC, and CI/CD definitions
 
 **Status:** Can run in parallel with Phases 4 to 6. Demo delivery mode covers authoring and static validation. Deploying anything to Azure still needs the user ([ADR-0007](./architecture/decisions/adr-0007-demo-delivery-mode.md)).
 
 **Goal:** Show the intended Azure architecture as validated Bicep, plus GitHub Actions pipelines for IaC and for application build and deployment.
 
 **Work packages:**
 
 1. **Bicep (`infra/bicep/`).** Add a subscription-scope `main.bicep` that creates the resource group, and modules for:
    * Network: VNet, subnets for Container Apps and private endpoints, NSGs, and NAT Gateway.
    * Platform services: Log Analytics, Application Insights, Key Vault, and ACR.
    * A Container Apps environment with `api` and `web` apps and a scheduled ingestion job (cron, weekly).
    * Cosmos DB for MongoDB, a Storage queue, and Azure AI Search, each with a private endpoint and a private DNS zone.
    * A user-assigned managed identity with least-privilege role assignments.
    * Foundry endpoint and deployment names as parameters. Never put secrets in parameters.
 
    Use pinned AVM modules where they fit (see `.github/agents/azure-verified-modules-bicep.agent.md` and `.github/instructions/bicep-code-best-practices.instructions.md`). Add `parameters/dev.bicepparam` and a `bicepconfig.json`. APIM is optional: include it as a module behind a `deployApim` boolean, default `false`, because of its cost.
 2. **Naming and tags.** Add a short table in `infra/README.md` with the pattern `{type}-psa-{env}-cac-{nn}` and the mandatory tags.
 3. **IaC pipeline (`.github/workflows/infra.yml`).** On a pull request to `infra/**`, run `bicep build`, `bicep lint`, and `az deployment sub what-if` (what-if needs OIDC secrets; skip it when they are absent). A deploy job runs on `workflow_dispatch` only, uses the `dev` environment, and authenticates with OIDC (`azure/login`).
 4. **App pipeline (`.github/workflows/app.yml`).** Run the Python and web checks, build the container images, and push to ACR on `main`. Deploy to Container Apps on `workflow_dispatch` with the `dev` environment.
 5. **Pinning.** Pin all actions by full SHA (follow `.github/instructions/ci-security.instructions.md`). Use `permissions: contents: read` by default, with `id-token: write` only on jobs that need it.
 6. **Bootstrap doc.** Document the one-time Entra app registration and federated credentials in `infra/README.md`.
 
 **Exit criteria:** `bicep build` and `bicep lint` pass locally. `actionlint` passes on all workflows. `what-if` runs if the subscription is available; otherwise record that it was skipped. The architecture overview's deployment diagram matches the Bicep.
 
 **Production-only (recorded, not done here):** PSRule or Checkov policy gates, the custom structural checks (CIDR overlap, DNS pairing), actual network-slice deployment and teardown, a detailed cost estimate, APIM SKU selection, and branch protection with required reviewers.
 
 ### Phase 8: Cloud deployment and pilot (not in demo scope)
 
 Deploying the application stack to Azure and running a pilot requires the user. It needs a budget, a chosen APIM SKU, and the production-only items from Phases 4 to 7. The Phase 7 pipelines make it a `workflow_dispatch` away once approved.

 There is currently no `infra/` directory or deployed Azure application stack.
 The Azure architecture and future infrastructure work are documented in the

 ## Architecture and data flow
 
 1. The source worker reads only
    [`phase-3-source-map-v1.json`](docs/operations/phase-3-source-map-v1.json)
    and stores permitted canonical pages and fetch state in local MongoDB.
 2. `scripts/index_documents.py` creates or updates a versioned Azure AI Search
    index and writes chunks/vectors using the Foundry embedding deployment.
 3. The browser sends chat requests to Next.js. The server-side route calls
    FastAPI; the agent retrieves filtered evidence from Azure AI Search and
    calls the Foundry chat deployment.
 4. The API binds cited evidence IDs to retrieved source URLs. The UI renders
    answers as plain text and links from the citation list only.
 
 See the [architecture overview](docs/architecture/architecture-overview.md)
 for diagrams and [ADR-0005](docs/architecture/decisions/adr-0005-ui-and-backend-technology.md)
 for the UI/backend boundary.

 ## Control posture
 
 | Control area | Local MVP: planned to demonstrate | Cloud target: design-only |
 |---|---|---|
 | Source access | Host allowlist, versioned source map, `robots.txt`, URL validation, no authentication, no redirects, bounded requests and downloads, durable fetch state | Scheduled Container Apps job; worker egress through approved NAT Gateway or firewall; host allowlist and stable egress |
 | Protected resources | Skip 401/403, login redirects, and login-content responses; record minimal reason | Same application behavior plus private network controls where applicable |
 | Retrieval and citations | Server-side evidence IDs and source URLs; reject citations not bound to retrieval | APIM and service identity controls do not replace application citation validation |
 | Prompt injection | Treat retrieved text as data; restrict tools; validate tool inputs and model output | Same application controls with policy and monitoring integration |
 | Secrets | Local environment/configuration outside source control; no credentials in fixtures, logs, or traces | Key Vault and managed identity where supported; GitHub Actions OIDC |
 | Network isolation | Segmented Podman networks if validated; local demo bound to local access | VNet, subnets, NSGs, private endpoints/DNS, controlled egress, APIM |
 | Search/data access | User-provided Azure AI Search; least-privilege Entra ID where supported; no shared production data | Private endpoint, RBAC, network restrictions, environment separation |
 | Telemetry | OpenTelemetry-compatible, minimized metadata; query/response content is not retained | Azure Monitor and Log Analytics with approved retention and access controls |
 | Supply chain | Dependency lock and scans, secret scanning, container scanning in CI | Pinned GitHub Actions, protected deployment environment, artifact provenance |
 | User access | Local-only demo with no end-user authentication; no public exposure | User authentication and authorization remain a Phase 7 design decision |
 | Cloud deployment | No application stack deployment | IaC static validation only; application deployment is deferred |
 
 ## Required evidence
 
 * Unit and integration tests must prove protected content is skipped, URLs are
   validated, citations resolve only to retrieved sources, and sensitive test
   values do not appear in logs or traces.
 * Phase 0b must map each trust boundary and asset to a rated threat, mitigation,
   owner, and verifying test.
 * Phase 7 checks must distinguish static IaC validation from deployed network
   evidence. The application stack remains undeployed.
 * Live source, Foundry, Azure AI Search, and subscription tests require explicit
   approval and isolated resources. Routine CI uses fakes or emulators.

 working local system over production readiness; their absence is an intentional
 demo-scope decision, not an untracked omission. Completing this register does

Use non-generic `Workflow` type and non-generic `Build()` method:

✅ **CORRECT Pattern** (use ExecutorCompletedEvent):

### Agent Type 
#### Agent Type Selection

**For .NET:**
**IMPORTANT**: When using Microsoft Foundry, always use `AIProjectClient` to create agents - NOT `AzureOpenAIClient`.
- ❌ Do NOT use `AzureOpenAIClient` for Microsoft Foundry models - that's only for testing and lacks conversation persistence
- ✅ DO use `AIProjectClient` - it provides full agent capabilities with service-managed state and is the latest recommended approach
- ⚠️ `PersistentAgentsClient` is a legacy client (deprecated) - use `AIProjectClient` instead

Code samples may show `AzureOpenAIClient` for simplicity or backward compatibility, but production implementations should use `AIProjectClient` for Microsoft Foundry.

#### Key Differences: AIProjectClient vs AzureOpenAIClient

**1. Creation Pattern:**
- `AIProjectClient` uses `await aiProjectClient.CreateAIAgentAsync(...)` - creates agents on the server
- `AzureOpenAIClient` uses `.GetChatClient(deploymentName).CreateAIAgent(...)` - creates local agents

#### ✅ CORRECT - AIProjectClient Pattern (Recommended)

```csharp
using System.ComponentModel;
using System.Text.Json.Serialization;
using Azure.AI.Projects;
using Azure.Identity;
using Microsoft.Agents.AI;
using Microsoft.Extensions.AI;

string endpoint = Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("AZURE_FOUNDRY_PROJECT_ENDPOINT") ?? throw new InvalidOperationException("AZURE_FOUNDRY_PROJECT_ENDPOINT is not set.");
string deploymentName = Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("AZURE_FOUNDRY_PROJECT_DEPLOYMENT_NAME") ?? "gpt-4o-mini";

[Description("Get the weather for a given location.")]
static string GetWeather([Description("The location to get the weather for.")] string location)
    => $"The weather in {location} is cloudy with a high of 15°C.";

const string AssistantInstructions = "You are a helpful assistant that can get weather information.";
const string AssistantName = "WeatherAssistant";

// Define structured output schema for weather response
[Description("Weather information for a location")]
public class WeatherResponse
{
    [JsonPropertyName("location")]
    public string Location { get; set; } = string.Empty;

    [JsonPropertyName("temperature")]
    public string Temperature { get; set; } = string.Empty;

    [JsonPropertyName("condition")]
    public string Condition { get; set; } = string.Empty;
}

// Get a client to create/retrieve/delete server side agents with Microsoft Foundry agents.
AIProjectClient aiProjectClient = new(new Uri(endpoint), new AzureCliCredential());

// Define the agent with function tools.
AITool tool = AIFunctionFactory.Create(GetWeather);

// Create AIAgent directly - Simple agent with tools for basic scenarios
AIAgent agent = await aiProjectClient.CreateAIAgentAsync(
    name: AssistantName,
    model: deploymentName,
    instructions: AssistantInstructions,
    tools: [tool]);

// Create ChatClientAgent - Advanced agent with structured output support via ResponseFormat
// Use this when you need structured JSON responses with schema validation
ChatClientAgent agent1 = await aiProjectClient.CreateAIAgentAsync(
    model: deploymentName,
    new ChatClientAgentOptions(name: AssistantName, instructions: AssistantInstructions, tools: [tool])
    {
        ChatOptions = new()
        {
            ResponseFormat = Microsoft.Extensions.AI.ChatResponseFormat.ForJsonSchema<WeatherResponse>()
        }
    });

// Non-streaming agent interaction with function tools.
Console.WriteLine(await agent.RunAsync("What is the weather like in Amsterdam?"));

// Streaming agent interaction with function tools.
await foreach (AgentRunResponseUpdate update in agent.RunStreamingAsync("What is the weather like in Amsterdam?"))
{
    Console.WriteLine(update);
}

// Cleanup: Delete the created agent instance by name.
await aiProjectClient.Agents.DeleteAgentAsync(agent.Name);
await aiProjectClient.Agents.DeleteAgentAsync(agent1.Name);



```

#### ❌ INCORRECT - AzureOpenAIClient Patterns to Avoid

**Don't use explicit thread management with AzureOpenAIClient:**
```csharp

// Create AIAgent with AzureOpenAIClient
AIAgent agent = new AzureOpenAIClient(new Uri(endpoint), new AzureCliCredential()) // ❌ WRONG: Use AIProjectClient instead
    .GetChatClient(deploymentName)
    .CreateAIAgent(instructions: "You are a helpful assistant");
```

#### ❌ INCORRECT - Don't Use Legacy PersistentAgentsClient Pattern

```csharp
using Azure.AI.Agents.Persistent;  // ❌ WRONG: Use Azure.AI.Projects instead

var client = new PersistentAgentsClient(  // ❌ WRONG: Use AIProjectClient instead

```

"*** Begin Patch
*** Add File: infra\README.md
+Scope note: this IaC is validated by build, lint and static review only and has not been deployed. It shows the intended Azure architecture. Production gates (policy scanning, structural checks, cost estimate, APIM SKU choice, branch protection) are recorded in the Phase 7 "Production-only" note and in `docs/operations/production-gap-register.md`. The focus was a working local application first.
+
+# Azure infrastructure design
+
+The subscription-scope template creates the resource group, then provisions the
+network, platform, data, identity, and Container Apps modules in Canada Central.
+`deployApim` defaults to `false`. The web app has external ingress, the API has
+internal ingress, private endpoints are linked to the VNet through private DNS,
+and the Container Apps subnet uses a NAT Gateway for outbound traffic. Foundry
+remains a public endpoint configured with parameters.
+
+The Container Apps templates reference these Key Vault secret names; create
+their values separately before running workloads. No secret values belong in
+Bicep or parameter files:
+
+* `mongodb-connection-string`
+* `azure-ai-search-api-key`
+* `azure-openai-api-key`
+
+The cloud image references and Foundry parameter values in
+`bicep/parameters/dev.bicepparam` are placeholders. The full template is
+design-only and is not a separately deployable network slice.
+
+## Naming
+
+Use `{type}-psa-{env}-cac-{nn}` for resource names where Azure permits it.
+Resources with restricted character sets or shorter maximum lengths preserve
+the same project, environment, region, and instance tokens in a compact name.
+Global resource names include a short deterministic suffix.
+
+| Name segment | Meaning | Example |
+|---|---|---|
+| `{type}` | Azure resource type abbreviation | `vnet`, `cae`, `pe` |
+| `psa` | Product Support Agent | `psa` |
+| `{env}` | Environment | `dev` |
+| `cac` | Canada Central | `cac` |
+| `{nn}` | Two-digit instance number | `01` |
+
+## Mandatory tags
+
+| Tag | Purpose | Template value |
+|---|---|---|
+| `application` | Workload identification | `product-support-agent` |
+| `costCenter` | Cost attribution | `costCenter` parameter (`TBD` placeholder) |
+| `environment` | Environment isolation | `environment` parameter |
+| `managedBy` | Infrastructure ownership | `bicep` |
+| `owner` | Operational ownership | `owner` parameter (`team-placeholder`) |
+
+## One-time GitHub OIDC bootstrap
+
+1. Register an Entra application and service principal for this repository's
+   deployment workflows. Create a federated credential with issuer
+   `https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com`, audience
+   `api://AzureADTokenExchange`, and subject
+   `repo:<OWNER>/<REPO>:environment:dev`. Do not create a client secret.
+2. Grant the application only the permissions required to create the target
+   resource group and deploy into the subscription. For image publishing, grant
+   `AcrPush` at the ACR scope only. Review and narrow deployment permissions
+   before production.
+3. Configure the GitHub `dev` environment and add these repository secrets by
+   name; do not put their values in this file:
+   `AZURE_CLIENT_ID`, `AZURE_TENANT_ID`, `AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID`.
+4. Add these repository variables by name for the application workflow:
+   `ACR_NAME`, `RESOURCE_GROUP_NAME`, `API_CONTAINER_APP_NAME`,
+   `WEB_CONTAINER_APP_NAME`.
+
+The `dev` environment protects image publication, what-if, and manual
+deployment. The `infra` workflow deploys only on `workflow_dispatch`; the
+`app` workflow deploys Container Apps only on `workflow_dispatch` and publishes
+images only from `main`. Configure environment reviewers and the federated
+subject to match the repository before enabling OIDC.
+
+## Validation boundary
+
+Run `az bicep build --file infra/bicep/main.bicep`,
+`az bicep build-params --file infra/bicep/parameters/dev.bicepparam`, and
+`az bicep lint --file infra/bicep/main.bicep` before review. The workflows
+repeat static checks. Deployment and resource changes are outside this
+validation boundary.

| Developer | **Container Registry Tasks Contributor** | ACR | Remote build path (`docker.remoteBuild: true` -- the default) |
| Developer | **Container Registry Repository Writer** | ACR | ABAC-mode ACR, local build path |
| Developer | **Owner** or **Contributor** | ACR | ABAC-mode ACR, remote build path (Repository Writer doesn't cover Tasks) |
| Project managed identity (system-assigned on the Foundry project) | **AcrPull** | ACR | Always -- granted automatically by `azd deploy` |

Run `azd ai agent doctor` after a deploy attempt to see the RBAC state. Failed pushes also surface the missing role and a paste-ready `az role assignment create` command.
## Work with a private endpoint on the ACR
If the ACR has `publicNetworkAccess: Disabled`, and is only reachable from a virtual network, then `azd up` must run from inside that virtual network. Use a self-hosted runner, an Azure DevOps agent, or a jump host.
The Foundry runtime separately needs network reachability to the registry to pull the image. That requirement is a platform concern beyond this article.
See [Configure virtual networks](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/virtual-networks) for the network-side picture and for how to integrate this workflow with private endpoints on the ACR, Foundry account, AppInsights, and Storage.","contentUrl":"https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/deploy-hosted-agent-private-azure-container-registry#review-rbac"},{"title":"Connect privately to an Azure container registry by using Azure Private Link","content":"# Connect privately to an Azure container registry by using Azure Private Link
## Disable public access to a registry
For many scenarios, disable registry access from public networks. This configuration prevents all clients outside the virtual network from reaching the registry endpoints.
To disable public access to a container registry in the Azure portal, follow these steps:
1. In your container registry's service menu, under **Settings**, select **Networking**.
2. On the **Public access** tab, in **Public network access**, select **Disabled**. Then select **Save**.
You can also use the Azure CLI to disable public access by running [az acr update](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cli/azure/acr#az-acr-update) and set `--public-network-enabled` to `false`.
Note
If you disable public access to a registry, `az acr build` commands no longer work.
```azurecli
az acr update --name $REGISTRY_NAME --public-network-enabled false
```
## Use `az acr build` with private endpoint and private registry
Note
If you disable public network access, `az acr build` commands will fail. Unless you use dedicated agent pools, public IPs are typically required. Tasks reserve a set of public IPs in each region for outbound requests. If needed, you can add these IPs to your firewall's allowed list for seamless communication. `az acr build` command uses the same set of IPs as tasks.
Consider the following options to execute the `az acr build` successfully.
1. Assign a [dedicated agent pool](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/container-registry/tasks-agent-pools).
2. If agent pool isn't available in your region, add the regional [Azure Container Registry Service Tag IPv4](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/service-tags-overview#use-the-service-tag-discovery-api) to the [firewall access rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/container-registry/container-registry-firewall-rules#allow-access-by-ip-address-range). Tasks reserve a set of public IPs in each region (`AzureContainerRegistry` service tag) for outbound requests. You can add these IPs to the firewall allowed list.","contentUrl":"https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/container-registry/container-registry-private-endpoints#disable-public-access-to-a-registry"},{"title":"Tutorial: Build and deploy container images in the cloud with Azure Container Registry Tasks","content":"# Tutorial: Build and deploy container images in the cloud with Azure Container Registry Tasks

## Tasks
### What git repository management service does Tasks support?
| Git service | Source context | Manual build | Auto build through commit trigger| 
|  --- | --- | --- | ---  |
| GitHub | `https://github.com/user/myapp-repo.git#mybranch:myfolder` | Yes | Yes |
| Azure Repos | `https://dev.azure.com/user/myproject/_git/myapp-repo#mybranch:myfolder` | Yes | Yes |
| GitLab | `https://gitlab.com/user/myapp-repo.git#mybranch:myfolder` | Yes | No |
| BitBucket | `https://user-edb9da08@example.com/user/mayapp-repo.git#mybranch:myfolder` | Yes | No |

### Why do I see an error saying no subscriptions were found?
You might see an error saying that no access was configured, so no subscriptions were found when using `az login --identity` in your ACR Task. This error is generally transient and occurs when the role assignment of your managed identity isn't propagated yet. Wait a few seconds before retrying.
### Is it expected for a build step to run with elevated privileges?
Yes. Build steps can run with elevated privileges in an isolated sandbox environment. See [Task execution and isolation](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/container-registry/container-registry-tasks-overview#task-execution-and-isolation).
### Where can I find sample CI/CD integration with ACR Tasks?
You can find sample CI/CD integration with ACR Tasks in the following links:
1. [CircleCI](https://github.com/Azure/acr/blob/master/docs/integration/CircleCI.md)
2. [GitHub Actions](https://github.com/Azure/acr/blob/master/docs/integration/github-actions/github-actions.md)
### How can I resolve agent pool creation failure due to time-out issues?
Set up the correct [firewall rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/container-registry/tasks-agent-pools#add-firewall-rules) to the existing network security groups or user-defined routes. After the setup, wait a few minutes for the firewall rules to apply.","contentUrl":"https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/container-registry/container-registry-faq#what-git-repository-management-service-does-tasks-support"},{"title":"Automate container image builds and maintenance with Azure Container Registry tasks","content":"# Automate container image builds and maintenance with Azure Container Registry tasks
## Automatically triggered tasks
Enable one or more *triggers* to build an image.
### Trigger a task on a source code update
You can trigger a container image build or multi-step task when code is committed, or a pull request is made or updated, to a public or private Git repository in GitHub or Azure DevOps. For example, configure a build task with the Azure CLI command [az acr task create](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cli/azure/acr/task#az-acr-task-create) by specifying a Git repository and optionally a branch and Dockerfile. When your team updates code in the repository, a webhook created in Azure Container Registry tasks triggers a build of the container image defined in the repo.
Azure Container Registry tasks support the following triggers when you set a Git repo as a task's context:
| Trigger | Enabled by default| 
|  --- | ---  |
| Commit | Yes |
| Pull request | No |

Note
Currently, Azure Container Registry tasks don't support commit or pull-request triggers in GitHub Enterprise repos.
To learn how to trigger builds on source code commits, see [Automate container image builds with Azure Container Registry tasks](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/container-registry/container-registry-tutorial-build-task).
#### Personal access token
To configure a trigger for source code updates, you need to provide the task a personal access token to set the webhook in the public or private GitHub or Azure DevOps repo. Required scopes for the personal access token are as follows:
| Repo type | GitHub | Azure DevOps| 
|  --- | --- | ---  |
| Public repo | repo:statuspublic\_repo | Code (Read) |
| Private repo | repo (Full control) | Code (Read) |

To create a personal access token, see the [GitHub](https://docs.github.com/en/github/authenticating-to-github/keeping-your-account-and-data-secure/creating-a-personal-access-token) or [Azure DevOps](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/organizations/accounts/use-personal-access-tokens-to-authenticate) documentation.
### Automate OS and framework patching
The power of Azure Container Registry tasks to enhance your container build workflow comes from their ability to detect an update to a *base image*. A base image is a feature of most container images. It's a parent image on which one or more application images are based. Base images typically contain the operating system and sometimes application frameworks.","contentUrl":"https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/container-registry/container-registry-tasks-overview#automatically-triggered-tasks"},{"title":"ACR Tasks reference: YAML","content":"# ACR Tasks reference: YAML

I configured the following properties at ACR.
Here is part of the task error log
##Accepted Answers:
Hello Yu Ding.
Thank you for sharing the details and logs. Based on the error message and your current Azure Container Registry (ACR) configuration, this behavior is expected and is related to how ACR Tasks interact with network‑restricted registries.
Your ACR Task is failing during the login step with the error:
“denied: client with IP '<ip>' is not allowed access”</ip>
Although publicNetworkAccess is enabled and networkRuleBypassAllowedForTasks is set to true, ACR Tasks run from Microsoft‑managed infrastructure using dynamic outbound IP addresses. These IPs are not automatically exempted by firewall rules unless one of the supported access models is explicitly configured.
Microsoft documentation confirms that:
ACR Tasks are no longer implicitly treated as trusted services
Network bypass must be explicitly enabled and validated
Otherwise, the registry firewall will reject task traffic, resulting in 403 / denied errors.
Actions to perform:
Use a Dedicated Agent Pool
Run ACR Tasks using a dedicated agent pool deployed into your virtual network. This allows tasks to access the registry through private connectivity, avoiding public IP restrictions entirely.
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-registry/manage-network-bypass-policy-for-tasks
Allow ACR Service Tag IPs in Firewall Rules:
If public access is required, explicitly allow the AzureContainerRegistry service tag IP ranges for your region in the ACR firewall. These are the outbound IPs used by ACR Tasks.
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/azure/azure-container-registry/client-ip-address-not-allowed-access
IP ranges are region‑specific and may change.
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-registry/container-registry-firewall-access-rules
Requires ongoing maintenance.
The registry firewall still evaluates the task’s outbound IP, and if it’s not explicitly permitted, access is denied. This is a documented and intentional security behavior.
If the issue persists after applying the above recommendation, we are more than happy to assist further. Please add your comments in the Comment section, and we will get back to you promptly to continue the investigation.
Thanks.","contentUrl":"https://learn.microsoft.com/answers/a/12654355"},{"title":"Run ACR Tasks using Resource Manager templates","content":"# Run ACR Tasks using Resource Manager templates
[ACR Tasks](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/container-registry/container-registry-tasks-overview) is a suite of features within Azure Container Registry to help you manage and modify container images across the container lifecycle.
This article shows Azure Resource Manager template examples to queue a quick task run, similar to one you can create manually using the [az acr build](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cli/azure/acr#az-acr-build) command.
A Resource Manager template to queue a task run is useful in automation scenarios and extends the functionality of `az acr build`. For example:
1. Use a template to create a container registry and immediately queue a task run to build and push a container image
2. Create or enable additional resources you can use in a quick task run, such as a managed identity for Azure resources
## Limitations
1. You must specify a remote context such as a GitHub repo as the [source location](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/container-registry/container-registry-tasks-overview#context-locations) for your task run. You can't use a local source context.
2. For task runs using a managed identity, only a *user-assigned* managed identity is permitted.
## Prerequisites
1. **GitHub account** - Create an account on https://github.com if you don't already have one.
2. **Fork sample repository** - For the task examples shown here, use the GitHub UI to fork the following sample repository into your GitHub account: https://github.com/Azure-Samples/acr-build-helloworld-node. This repo contains sample Dockerfiles and source code to build small container images.","contentUrl":"https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/container-registry/container-registry-task-run-template"},{"title":"Tutorial: Automate container image builds in the cloud when you commit source code","content":"# Tutorial: Automate container image builds in the cloud when you commit source code

Use a centrally managed Azure Container Registry (ACR) when you deploy hosted agent container images. You can build locally and push to an existing ACR, or skip the build and deploy a pre-built image that was pushed by another pipeline.
If you use a coding agent like GitHub Copilot, the [Microsoft Foundry Skill](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/foundry/how-to/develop/use-microsoft-foundry-skill) can help you choose an ACR workflow, prepare the required permissions, and apply the deployment steps for your project.
## Prerequisites
1. An initialized hosted agent project with an `azure.yaml` file. For setup, see [Initialize an agent project](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/init-agent-project).
2. The [azd Foundry extensions installed](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/install-cli-foundry-extensions).
3. An authenticated `azd` session.
4. Access to an existing Azure Container Registry.
5. Required ACR permissions for your selected build path.
## Choose your ACR workflow
Most teams want their hosted agent container images to come from a centrally managed ACR, not a new per-project registry. There are two flavors of this:
1. **Build locally and push** to an existing ACR. This is typical when teams share one registry across many projects.
2. **Skip the build entirely** and deploy a pre-built image that was already pushed by a separate pipeline.
Note
Both workflows are independent of whether the ACR is "private" in the network sense, such as a private endpoint with `publicNetworkAccess: Disabled`. Network privacy is covered in [Configure virtual networks](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/virtual-networks). This article focuses on registry selection and access.","contentUrl":"https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/deploy-hosted-agent-private-azure-container-registry"}]}

1. **Build locally and push** to an existing ACR. This is typical when teams share one registry across many projects.

Note
Both workflows are independent of whether the ACR is "private" in the network sense, such as a private endpoint with `publicNetworkAccess: Disabled`. ## Decide when to bring your own ACR
Bring your own ACR when one or more of these requirements apply:
1. **Compliance.** Images must live in a centrally audited registry your org already operates.
2. **Shared infrastructure.** One ACR feeds many agent projects; new per-project registries aren't acceptable.
3. **ABAC-mode registries.** Your enterprise ACR is configured with attribute-based access control, requiring specific roles.
4. **Pre-built images.** A separate CI pipeline builds the image with vulnerability scanning, supply-chain signing, and hardened base images. The agent project should consume that image as-is.
If none of those apply, leave the defaults alone. `azd ai agent init` creates a new ACR for the project and `azd up` pushes to it.
## Review registry selection
When you run `azd ai agent init` against an existing Microsoft Foundry project, the extension scans the project for ACR connections and offers them as choices:
1. **0 ACR connections found.** You're prompted for an ACR authentication server, such as `myregistry.azurecr.io`. Leave the prompt blank to let `azd provision` create the project registry when your configuration requires one.
2. **1 ACR connection found.** It's selected automatically and shown in the output.
3. **2+ ACR connections found.** You pick one from a list.
Whatever is selected writes two env vars to your azd environment:
| Environment variable | What it is| 
|  --- | ---  |
| `AZURE_CONTAINER_REGISTRY_ENDPOINT` | Authentication server, for example `myregistry.azurecr.io` |
| `AZURE_CONTAINER_REGISTRY_RESOURCE_ID` | Full ARM resource ID. Optional, but enables faster, scoped RBAC preflight checks. |

You can also set these environment variables yourself before `azd up`:
```bash
azd env set AZURE_CONTAINER_REGISTRY_ENDPOINT myregistry.azurecr.io
azd env set AZURE_CONTAINER_REGISTRY_RESOURCE_ID \
  /subscriptions/<sub>/resourceGroups/<rg>/providers/Microsoft.ContainerRegistry/registries/myregistry
```
When both are set, `azd` skips creating a new ACR and the build path pushes directly to the existing one.","contentUrl":"https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/deploy-hosted-agent-private-azure-container-registry#decide-when-to-bring-your-own-acr"},{"title":"Secure your Azure Container Registry deployment","content":"# Secure your Azure Container Registry deployment
## Network security
By default a registry is reachable over the public internet. Restricting network access is one of the most effective ways to reduce the attack surface, and the strongest controls require the Premium service tier.
1. **Connect to the registry through a private endpoint**: Use Azure Private Link to assign the registry a private IP address in your virtual network and keep pull and push traffic off the public internet. Private endpoints require the Premium service tier. For more information, see [Connect private<output too long - dropped 15085 characters from the middle> registry and Save highlighted.](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/deployment-environments/media/how-to-configure-extensibility-bicep-container-image/container-registry-network-disable-public.png)](media/how-to-configure-extensibility-bicep-container-image/container-registry-network-disable-public.png#lightbox)
#### Assign the AcrPull role
Creating environments by using container images uses the ADE infrastructure, including projects and environment types. Each project has one or more project environment types, which need read access to the container image that defines the environment to be deployed. To access the images within your ACR securely, assign the AcrPull role to each project environment type.
To assign the AcrPull role to the Project Environment Type:
1. In the Azure portal, go to the ACR that you want to configure.
2. On the left menu, select **Access Control (IAM)**.
3. Select **Add** > **Add role assignment**.
4. Assign the following role. For detailed steps, see [Assign Azure roles using the Azure portal](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/role-based-access-control/role-assignments-portal).
 | Setting | Value |

 | **Role** | Select **AcrPull**. |
 | **Assign access to** | Select **User, group, or service principal**. |
 | **Members** | Enter the name of the project environment type that needs to access the image in the container. |
 The project environment type displays like the following example:
 [![Screenshot of the Select members pane, showing a list of project environment types with part of the name highlighted.](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/deployment-environments/media/how-to-configure-extensibility-bicep-container-image/container-registry-access-control.png)](media/how-to-configure-extensibility-bicep-container-image/container-registry-access-control.png#lightbox)
In this configuration, ADE uses the Managed Identity for the PET, whether system assigned or user assigned.
Tip
This role assignment has to be made for every project environment type. It can be automated through the Azure CLI.
Tip
If your ACR uses Microsoft Entra attribute-based access control (ABAC) for repository permissions, you may need to make additional role assignments like `Container Registry Repository Reader` to the PET identity. For more information, see [Microsoft Entra ABAC for repository permissions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-registry/container-registry-rbac-abac-repository-permissions).

## Troubleshoot ACR deployment
| Symptom | Cause | What to try| 
|  --- | --- | ---  |

If you use a coding agent like GitHub Copilot, the [Microsoft Foundry Skill](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/foundry/how-to/develop/use-microsoft-foundry-skill) can help you choose an ACR workflow, prepare the required permissions, and apply the deployment steps for your project.
## Prerequisites
1. An initialized hosted agent project with an `azure.yaml` file. For setup, see [Initialize an agent project](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/init-agent-project).
2. The [azd Foundry extensions installed](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/install-cli-foundry-extensions).
3. An authenticated `azd` session.
4. Access to an existing Azure Container Registry.
5. Required ACR permissions for your selected build path.
## Choose your ACR workflow
Most teams want their hosted agent container images to come from a centrally managed ACR, not a new per-project registry. There are two flavors of this:
1. **Build locally and push** to an existing ACR. This is typical when teams share one registry across many projects.
2. **Skip the build entirely** and deploy a pre-built image that was already pushed by a separate pipeline.
Note
Both workflows are independent of whether the ACR is "private" in the network sense, such as a private endpoint with `publicNetworkAccess: Disabled`. ## Decide when to bring your own ACR
Bring your own ACR when one or more of these requirements apply:
1. **Compliance.** Images must live in a centrally audited registry your org already operates.
2. **Shared infrastructure.** One ACR feeds many agent projects; new per-project registries aren't acceptable.
3. **ABAC-mode registries.** Your enterprise ACR is configured with attribute-based access control, requiring specific roles.
4. **Pre-built images.** A separate CI pipeline builds the image with vulnerability scanning, supply-chain signing, and hardened base images. The agent project should consume that image as-is.
If none of those apply, leave the defaults alone. `azd ai agent init` creates a new ACR for the project and `azd up` pushes to it.
## Review registry selection
When you run `azd ai agent init` against an existing Microsoft Foundry project, the extension scans the project for ACR connections and offers them as choices:
1. **0 ACR connections found.** You're prompted for an ACR authentication server, such as `myregistry.azurecr.io`. Leave the prompt blank to let `azd provision` create the project registry when your configuration requires one.
2. **1 ACR connection found.** It's selected automatically and shown in the output.
3. **2+ ACR connections found.** You pick one from a list.
Whatever is selected writes two env vars to your azd environment:
| Environment variable | What it is| 
|  --- | ---  |
| `AZURE_CONTAINER_REGISTRY_ENDPOINT` | Authentication server, for example `myregistry.azurecr.io` |
| `AZURE_CONTAINER_REGISTRY_RESOURCE_ID` | Full ARM resource ID. Optional, but enables faster, scoped RBAC preflight checks. |

You can also set these environment variables yourself before `azd up`:
```bash
azd env set AZURE_CONTAINER_REGISTRY_ENDPOINT myregistry.azurecr.io
azd env set AZURE_CONTAINER_REGISTRY_RESOURCE_ID \
  /subscriptions/<sub>/resourceGroups/<rg>/providers/Microsoft.ContainerRegistry/registries/myregistry
```
When both are set, `azd` skips creating a new ACR and the build path pushes directly to the existing one.","contentUrl":"https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/deploy-hosted-agent-private-azure-container-registry#decide-when-to-bring-your-own-acr"},{"title":"Secure your Azure Container Registry deployment","content":"# Secure your Azure Container Registry deployment
## Network security
By default a registry is reachable over the public internet. Restricting network access is one of the most effective ways to reduce the attack surface, and the strongest controls require the Premium service tier.
1. **Connect to the registry through a private endpoint**: Use Azure Private Link to assign the registry a private IP address in your virtual network and keep pull and push traffic off the public internet. Private endpoints require the Premium service tier. For more information, see [Connect privately to a container registry using Azure Private Link](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/container-registry/container-registry-private-endpoints).
2. **Disable public network access**: After private connectivity is in place, set public network access to disabled so the registry is reachable only through its private endpoints. For more information, see [Disable public access to a registry](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/container-registry/container-registry-private-endpoints#disable-public-access-to-a-registry).
3. **Restrict access to selected public IP addresses when public access is required**: Configure IP network rules to allow only known public IP ranges, such as your build agents or egress addresses, and deny all others. Selected-network rules require the Premium service tier. For more information, see [Configure public IP network rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/container-registry/container-registry-access-selected-networks).
4. **Allow only the trusted Azure services that need registry access**: The trusted-services bypass lets select Microsoft services reach a network-restricted registry. Enable it only for services you actually use, such as Azure Container Instances, Microsoft Defender for Cloud, or Machine Learning. For more information, see [Allow trusted services to access a network-restricted registry](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/container-registry/allow-access-trusted-services).
5. **Disable the network-rule bypass for ACR Tasks unless a task requires it**: Prevent ACR Tasks from bypassing the registry's network rules so that automated builds are subject to the same restrictions as other clients. For more information, see [Manage the network bypass policy for tasks](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/container-registry/manage-network-bypass-policy-for-tasks).
6. **Account for regional endpoints when configuring firewall rules**: When you restrict outbound access from clients or use geo-replication, allow the global registry endpoint and each required regional data endpoint so that pulls aren't silently blocked. Run `azd ai agent doctor` after a deploy attempt to see the RBAC state. Failed pushes also surface the missing role and a paste-ready `az role assignment create` command.
## Work with a private endpoint on the ACR
If the ACR has `publicNetworkAccess: Disabled`, and is only reachable from a virtual network, then `azd up` must run from inside that virtual network. Use a self-hosted runner, an Azure DevOps agent, or a jump host.
The Foundry runtime separately needs network reachability to the registry to pull the image. That requirement is a platform concern beyond this article.

## Deploy a pre-built image
Use this workflow when a separate CI pipeline already builds, scans, signs, and pushes the image. The agent project consumes that image directly, with no Dockerfile and no local build.
1. Set the `image` field in the `azure.ai.agent` service in `azure.yaml`.
```yaml
 services:
   my-agent:
     host: azure.ai.agent
     project: src/my-agent
     kind: hosted
     name: my-agent
     image: myregistry.azurecr.io/agents/my-agent:1.2.3
     env:
       PYTHONNOUSERSITE: "1"
     protocols:
       - protocol: responses
         version: "2.0.0"
```
 The `image` value must be a valid container reference. Both tags and SHA digests are accepted. Pin to a digest (`@sha256:...`) for reproducible deploys.
 The environment setting shown is for Python images; omit it for other runtimes. See [Configure Python startup](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/configure-hosted-agent-env-variables#configure-python-startup) for dependency compatibility.
 For a new project, provide the image during initialization instead:
```bash
 azd ai agent init --image myregistry.azurecr.io/agents/my-agent:1.2.3 --agent-name my-agent
```
 The `--image` option uses the prebuilt image path and skips code scaffolding, Dockerfile generation, and ACR setup.
2. Run the deploy.
```bash
 azd deploy

 # Or run up end-to-end
 azd up
```
 The Foundry hosted agent runtime pulls the image from your ACR using the **project managed identity**, which `azd` granted **AcrPull** during deploy. The per-agent agent identity isn't used for image pulls.
### Select an existing project connection noninteractively
For a container build against an existing Foundry project, use `--acr-connection <connection-name>` during initialization to select its ACR connection. This option doesn't apply to source-code deployment or a prebuilt `--image`.
For a private prebuilt image, select the registry connection instead:
```bash
azd ai agent init --agent-name my-agent \
  --image myregistry.azurecr.io/agents/my-agent:1.2.3 \
  --registry-connection <connection-name>
```
The connection must already exist. This workflow is the most common enterprise path: keep the default container build, but target a shared registry instead of a per-project one.
1. Point at the existing ACR.

 `azd up` runs a preflight check against the ACR before it starts building. The role you need depends on which build path is configured in `azure.yaml`:
 | Build path | Required developer role on the ACR |
 | --- | --- |
 | **Local build** (`docker.remoteBuild: false`) | **AcrPush** -- data-plane push of the locally built image |
 | **Remote build** (`docker.remoteBuild: true`, the default) | **Container Registry Tasks Contributor** -- needed to call `listBuildSourceUploadUrl` and `scheduleRun` |

2.1. Local build: **Container Registry Repository Writer** (per-repository grant), or
2.2. Remote build: **Owner**/**Contributor**, since the Repository Writer role doesn't cover ACR Tasks actions.
When the push or remote build fails with a 403, `azd up` classifies the error and prints a ready-to-paste `az role assignment create` command, substituting your object ID and the ACR scope from the ARM error response.
3. Run `azd up`.
```bash
 azd up
```
 The build artifact is pushed to your existing ACR.
